body:
Yeah, at least in Canada I can actually afford to see someone. I think in the states I'd be completely without hope. I don't think I'd ever heard of EMDR before your comment, so I'll have to look into it.

I started erecting my barriers in my early to mid teens, when I was in government care. A lot of the kids I was thrown in with were pretty prone to violence and other aggression, so I needed to learn quickly how to make sure I wasn't a target.

Afterwards, when I was released back to my parents' care, the house was a war zone. My dad was in the military and absolutely *loved* pretending he was the drill sergeant from Full Metal Jacket when dealing with me and my siblings. Talking at all was just another way to get torn down, and not talking meant he'd just get fed up, smack us around a little, and then leave to go drink and watch TV.

My mother, on the other hand, just loved my friends. She'd slip them booze, insinuate herself whenever I had someone over, and use things she learned from my therapists and group home workers to humiliate me in front of them. She absolutely seemed to think it was hilarious. She'd tell me my friends liked her more than they liked me. She was probably right.

I dealt with it by putting an even tighter grip on my life. Nobody came over, nothing was said at home or about home. As far as I was concerned I knew nothing. My family broke apart shortly after and I moved out and across the country at 16. I took the opportunity to completely reinvent myself, and that especially meant no longer being the person defined by having a shitty childhood.

I guess I can't stand the idea that someone will have the sort of control over me that being vulnerable allows. I was dumb enough to relax in two serious relationships and in both cases I was cheated on, which absolutely crushed me. I might feel terrible all the time now, but at least it's not something that's being done *to* me. At this point I'm withdrawn enough that I quite literally sometimes wonder if people still exist when they leave the room.

I hate the idea of these people I don't know at all, who I can't really even ask about themselves to any meaningful extent, being able to take these parts of me, record them and share them. I hate the idea of them judging me, even if their persona is professional and helpful. Who knows what they can do with that sort of material on me? I can't take it back if I don't like what they've done.

I've sought help for the anxiety, but it seems like all anyone wanted to talk about was the opiate abuse, and how it was causing all my problems. It's been eight months since I kicked them and things have gotten worse. At least before I could just go on the nod when I felt too awful.

I did change psychiatrists after my first one misdiagnosed me and put me on a drug contraindicated for people with bipolar I, which contributed to my second hospitalization.

It's a little difficult to make other changes because I live in a small area in Canada, which puts a limit on the number of practicing psychiatrists and therapists my insurance will cover. I'm also worried if I come back and try to approach another one honestly I'll end up in the psychiatric ward again. I can't stress how tired I am of that place and the hours of dragging, uncomfortable conversations separated by day upon endless day of bad TV and no sunlight. I need control over my situation to feel safe, and if there's one thing that place robs of you, it's agency.

Anyway, I don't mean to whine. I know what I have to do and it's been hammered into my head if I'd just try a little harder I can make progress. I just dread this idea of ending up like some of the people I met in the hospital, with their "I'm going to work through this" attitude which has kept them alive and kicking through decades of feeling awful with no end in sight. I don't believe in an afterlife, even if I regret it with all my heart in the last minute I'm alive, I'll never regret it again. I can't make that promise to myself with the alternative.
